june.name: June Calloway
june.role: geologist (a scientist who studies rocks and the land)

case.title: The Last Pit
case.hook: Fast-forward 20 years. The Palmetto Springs quarry is digging its very last pit, and the town has to decide what it becomes. Three designs are pinned on my drafting table. Which one should we build, and can we make it even better?

case.stillsCredit: The town, the designs and the costs are made up. Design B is like a real Florida project: the L-8 Reservoir, an old rock mine that now stores water.
case.question: Which design should Palmetto Springs build in the last pit, and how can they make it better?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: A limit is pass or fail, like the town’s $4 million budget. A goal gets scored: more stars is better.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: build the matrix
clues.t: The floating solar farm broke the budget limit, so it’s out. The bird lake and the reservoir tied at 6 stars.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: make it better
clues.t: Borrowing one feature from another design beat both first ideas, and it still fit the budget.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: test it small
clues.t: Testing a model showed two problems no one saw on paper. A spillway and a sloped shelf fixed them.

solve.title: What should the last pit become?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: The floating solar farm, because it got 3 stars for being useful.
options.why: Check Clue 2. Did the solar farm fit the budget?

options.t: Whichever design was pinned up first. The first idea is usually the best one.
options.why: Check Clue 3. Did the first ideas score as well as the improved one?

options.t: One of the tied designs, made better: borrow a feature from the other design, stay inside the budget, then test a model and revise it until it works.
options.why: Case cracked! You set limits and goals, compared, improved and tested, just like real engineers. Now write your case report: it’s the questions below.

limits.title: Limit or goal?
todo: Read the card from the town’s plan for the last pit.
Drag it to LIMIT or GOAL (or tap the card, then a box).
Sort all 8, then answer the question.

why.t: A limit is a gate: a design passes or fails. A goal is a score: a design can meet it well, just OK, or poorly.

limit.sub: Pass or fail. Yes or no.

cards.why: A design costs $4 million or less, or it doesn’t. Pass or fail.
cards.miss: Can a design be “a little bit” under budget and still get stars? Or is it yes or no?

cards.why: A design can help wildlife a lot, a little or barely. That’s a score.
cards.miss: Could one design help wildlife MORE than another? Then it’s scored.

cards.t: Edges must be gentle enough that no one can fall in
cards.why: Safe or not safe. There’s no “a little safe” for the town.
cards.miss: Is safety something the town would accept “just OK” on? Or is it yes or no?

cards.t: Stores water for the dry months
cards.why: A design can store lots of water, some, or a little. That’s a score.
cards.miss: Could one design store MORE water than another? Then it’s scored.

cards.why: It’s finished in 3 years, or it isn’t. Pass or fail.
cards.miss: A deadline is met or missed. Is that a score, or yes or no?

cards.t: Gives the town something useful, like power or a park
cards.why: Some designs give the town more than others. That’s a score.
cards.miss: Could one design be MORE useful than another? Then it’s scored.

cards.t: Can’t take water the town wells need
cards.why: The wells keep their water, or they don’t. Pass or fail.
cards.miss: Would the town accept a design that takes just a little of the wells’ water? Or is it yes or no?

cards.why: A design can look great, OK or not so nice. That’s a score.
cards.miss: Could one design look nicer than another? Then it’s scored.

limits.q: Which one is a LIMIT, not a goal?

opts.miss: Can a design help birds a lot or a little? Then it’s a goal.
Can a design look nicer or less nice? Then it’s a goal.

limits.win: Limits are pass or fail. Goals get scored. That’s a clue.

matrix.title: Build the matrix
todo: Tap a ? box. Read the evidence for that design and goal.
Fill every box, then check the budget limit.

why.t: The same kind of chart as the one above, now for the last pit in Palmetto Springs.

wild.fact: Shallow, planted edges give wading birds like herons and wood storks a place to feed and nest.

water.fact: A park lake is kept at about the same level, so it can’t save much extra water for dry months.

useful.fact: People could walk, fish and watch birds, but it makes no power and stores little water.

wild.fact: The water goes way up and down, and the sides are steep and deep, so few plants grow and few birds can feed.

water.fact: A deep rock pit can hold a huge amount of water. Florida’s L-8 Reservoir, an old rock mine, holds up to 15 billion gallons.

useful.fact: In dry months, stored water can be sent to the wetland. But there’s no park and no power.

wild.fact: Panels would cover much of the water, leaving little open water or shoreline for birds.

water.fact: The panels don’t make the pit store any extra water.

useful.fact: The panels would make clean electricity for many homes in town.

matrix.q: The bird lake and the reservoir tied. What should the engineers do next?

opts.t: Pick the solar farm. It got 3 stars for being useful.
opts.miss: Look at the budget row. Can the town afford it?
Engineers don’t guess. What could make one of them even better?

opts.t: Make one of them better by borrowing a feature from another design.

matrix.credit: L-8 Reservoir: Florida Department of Environmental Protection (a former rock mine site in Palm Beach County; 53 feet deep; stores up to 15 billion gallons). Palmetto Springs, its designs and their costs are made up for this lesson.
matrix.win: The solar farm broke the limit, and two designs tied. That’s a clue.

improve.title: Make it better
todo: Pick one of the tied designs.
Add features from the other designs. Watch the stars and the cost.
Get every goal to at least ⭐⭐ and stay inside the budget.

adds.why: A planted shelf gives birds a shallow place to feed, even beside deep water.

adds.t: A deep middle to store extra water
adds.why: Digging the middle deeper lets the lake hold extra water for dry months.
Panels on part of the water make electricity, but they cost a lot.

adds.t: A walking trail and fishing dock
adds.why: A trail and dock let people enjoy the water.

improve.q: Why is your improved design better than either first idea?

opts.t: It costs the most, so it must be the best.
opts.miss: Look at the cost bar. Is spending more money a goal?

opts.t: It meets every goal at least OK and still fits the budget.
It was the first design on the table.
opts.miss: Did you keep the first design exactly as it was?

improve.win: You borrowed a feature and beat both first ideas, inside the budget. That’s a clue.

photos.kicker: Look closer · a real rock-pit reservoir
photos.title: An old rock mine that stores water
todo: Tap each number on the photo to read what it is.
Then match the clues to the labels below.

why.t: The L-8 Reservoir in Palm Beach County, seen from above. It was a rock mine. Now it stores water for the Everglades.

photos.alt: An aerial photo: a huge dark reservoir split by thin strips of land, a canal running along its right side, and pale bare ground on the left where rock is being dug.
photos.credit: L-8 Reservoir area, Palm Beach County: U.S. Geological Survey, The National Map orthoimagery

hotspots.label: The dark water
hotspots.t: Old rock pits, now full of water. The reservoir is about 53 feet deep and can hold up to 15 billion gallons.

hotspots.label: The thin strips of land
hotspots.t: Walls of earth split the reservoir into parts, so engineers can move water from one part to another.

hotspots.label: The long dark line
hotspots.t: A canal. It carries water into the reservoir during storms and out again in dry months.

hotspots.label: The pale ground
hotspots.t: Bare rock and sand where digging is still going on. The reservoir looked like this before it filled with water.

task.q: Match each clue to a label on the photo.
task.win: You read a real reservoir like an engineer. One old rock pit got a whole new job.

items.evid: The deep old pits store the water.

items.step: Walls that split it into parts
items.evid: Strips of earth split the reservoir into parts.
A canal moves water in and out.

items.step: What a pit looks like while digging
items.evid: The pale ground is where digging is still going on.

pilot.afterText: June built a model of the improved pit
pilot.title: Test it small
todo: Run the first test on the model and watch the water.
If something goes wrong, pick the revision that fixes it.
Run the test again. Then do the next test.

why.t: Engineers test small models before they build big projects like dams and harbors. A problem is much cheaper to fix on a model.

tests.name: A week of heavy rain
tests.problem: The water rose way over the planted shelf. The plants are drowning, and wading birds can’t stand in water that deep.

fixes.t: Plant taller grass on the shelf
fixes.miss: Tall grass still drowns if the water stays deep for weeks. What could stop the water from rising so high?

fixes.t: Add a spillway pipe so extra water flows out to the canal
fixes.why: A spillway lets extra water flow out, so the water can only rise so high.

fixes.miss: Then the birds lose their shallow spot. That undoes your improvement!

tests.pass: The extra water flowed out the spillway, and the shelf stayed shallow.

tests.name: A long dry spell
tests.problem: The water dropped below the flat shelf. The plants dried out, and the birds left.

fixes.t: Fill it with a hose every day
fixes.miss: That would use lots of drinking water. Is there a way to change the design instead?
A deeper middle doesn’t keep the flat shelf wet. What shape would keep part of it wet?

fixes.t: Make the shelf a gentle slope, so part of it stays wet at any water level
fixes.why: On a slope, some of the edge is always right at the water, whether it’s high or low.

tests.pass: Even with low water, the bottom of the slope stayed wet, and the plants kept growing.

pilot.q: Why test a small model before building the real thing?

opts.t: Problems show up early, when they’re cheap and easy to fix.
Models are more fun than real pits.
opts.miss: Maybe! But what did testing the model help you find?

opts.t: So you never have to revise.
opts.miss: You revised twice! What did the tests help you find?

pilot.win: Testing found two problems no one saw on paper, and each revision fixed one. That’s your last clue.

q1.C: Cost can be a limit. Which one is a goal and which is a limit?

q2.A: Defining the problem comes first. What is changing a design to make it better?
q2.B: A constraint is a limit. What is changing a design to make it better?

q3.B: Spending more isn’t a goal. Think about the matrix: what did comparing show?
q3.C: Comparing takes time. Think about the matrix: what did comparing show?

welcome.label: Welcome · the last pit
welcome.script: June here! Let’s jump twenty years into the future. The Palmetto Springs quarry is digging its very last pit, and the town has to decide what it becomes. A bird lake? A water reservoir? A floating solar farm? Today you’re my engineer. We’ll compare all three, pick one, and make it even better.

warmup.label: Warm-Up · limit or goal? (Clue 1)
warmup.script: Engineers sort a plan into two kinds of rules. A limit is pass or fail, like a budget. A goal gets scored, like helping wildlife. Read each card from the town’s plan and drop it in the right box. Then tell me what you think about the city water ideas.

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Act out “revise” by erasing and redrawing a quick sketch; hold up a ruler for “constraint”.

part2.label: Part 2 · build the matrix (Clues 2 and 3)
part2.script: Time to build a decision matrix for our last pit. Tap each question box, read the evidence, and give it one, two or three stars. Then check the budget. Something surprising happens! After that, pick a design and make it better.

part3.label: Part 3 · four Florida challenges
part3.script: Engineers in Florida face lots of challenges like ours. Tap each one to see the possible solutions, and the revision an engineer might make. Notice how many of the best ideas combine two solutions.

explore.label: Part 4 · test it small (Clue 4)
explore.script: Before we build the real thing, let’s test a model. Run the first test and watch the water. If something goes wrong, pick the revision that fixes it, then test again. Real engineers do this over and over.

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab: what should the last pit become, and how can the town make it better? Then answer two questions, build your own decision matrix in Part C, and write your CER. Your answers save as you type.

partc.label: Part C · build a decision matrix

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says that if we just pick the smartest scientist’s first idea, we’ll always get the best solution. Hmm. Think about the tie, the budget and the model tests. Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.notes: Celebrate the end of Quarter 2; tease 17.01 (natural hazards: what a storm changes).
closing.script: Case closed, engineer! You compared, improved and tested, and the last pit got a great new job. That wraps up the quarter, too. Next week, a brand-new kind of problem: what happens to Florida’s land when a big storm hits?

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain how engineers compare solutions and make the best one better?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: The solar farm was useful, but it broke the budget limit.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “solar farm”, “broke” and “budget limit”. Those words tell what happened and why. Small words like “the” and “but” don’t carry the idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
